extraction.venue: arXiv preprint, arXiv:2503.11745 [physics.soc-ph]. No journal publication is stated in the text.
extraction.document_type: Empirical network-science preprint (main text pp. 1-9, references, Supplementary Information pp. 1-50). Introduces the LobbyView database and analyzes it.
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 5,280 lines of the text file (172,891 chars), covering main text pp. 1-9, references, and SI Sections I-XIV (pp. 1-50), in six chunks. The text is OCR-style extraction with ligature errors, so quoted wording is approximate. Annotation file read in full: 217 items, all Highlights by Paul Goff, zero sticky notes, zero comments, no subjects. Annotation page numbers match printed page numbers. Paul's covered text is not reproduced verbatim (copyright limit on source text); each highlight is summarized by topic and can be located by page and index in the annotation JSON at C:/Users/pgoff/Documents/research/_annots/a0c3322fb2cd.json.
extraction.research_question: How does the US federal lobbying network (clients, registrants, lobbyists, government entities, legislators) evolve over time? Specifically: (a) what growth and attachment rules govern client-registrant ties; (b) how does the network adapt to crises and to election or administration cycles; (c) can LDA disclosure data support probabilistic analysis of lobbying pathways for individual bills, issues, or firms, demonstrated on the Stop Online Piracy Act (SOPA, 2011).
extraction.theory: Network science and statistical physics rather than a formal political-economy model. Preferential attachment and cumulative advantage (Barabasi-Albert; Price's Matthew effect) explain hierarchy in K-Street registrant client counts. Attachment and detachment are treated as countervailing forces that stabilize the network. A five-layer directed multipartite graph is used. The political business cycle (Nordhaus 1975) is the framing for election-synchronized targeting. Partisan polarization is measured with cosponsorship and co-association bipartisan indices.
extraction.identification: None causal. The analysis is descriptive. Event-timing associations (2007-08 financial crisis, HLOGA 2007, 9/11, COVID-19, presidential terms) are shown as overlays without a counterfactual or instrument. Null comparisons use a bipartite configuration model for clustering and component size (SI IX). The SOPA result is a single case study using conditional probability shifts against a baseline (main p. 8). The paper's own wording is 'supporting the hypothesis' and 'lobbying is strategic'.
extraction.data: LobbyView relational database built from LDA LD-2 quarterly/semiannual filings. Period 1999-2023. Analyzed sample: 1,277,411 filings (SI Fig S2). Full LobbyView holds more than 1.6 million reports covering about 87 billion USD (main p. 2; SI Fig S4 gives 87.5 billion). Unit of observation: the filing, aggregated into one directed multilayer network per year. Layers: clients, registrants (K-Street external firms and In-House departments), lobbyists, government entities (agencies and chambers), legislators (members of Congress). Example snapshot 2017 (Fig 1B): 10,694 clients, 4,405 registrants, 11,543 lobbyists, 128 government entities, 374 legislators. Industry sectors use NAICS 2-digit codes (20 sectors) via S&P Compustat, covering about 40% of clients. Issues: 79 LDA issue codes; bills extracted by regex. Legislator data: US Digital Service congressional database. External linkage: Compustat, BoardEx, Orbis, NOMINATE. SOPA case: 67 publicly traded firms lobbying in Q4 2011 (main Fig 4 caption).
extraction.method: Descriptive and empirical statistics on a time-indexed multilayer directed graph. Steps: (1) in- and out-degree CCDFs by layer; MLE fits of an augmented power law with exponential cutoff, a log-normal and a Weibull, with the power law preferred (Fig 2F, SI Fig S11). (2) Preferential attachment: attachment and detachment functions by registrant in-degree, cumulated, with linearity tested (Fig 2E, SI VIII.B). (3) Survival or retention probability by year and age-conditioned exit (SI VIII.A). (4) Pareto charts and Gini indices of monetary flow (SI V). (5) Issue and target portfolios: client-share matrices, year-to-year Spearman correlation, PCA (SI XI). (6) Bipartite clustering coefficients and largest connected component, against a configuration-model null (SI IX). (7) SOPA pathway probabilities: uniform client draw, conditional probability shift Delta P(sector | SOPA) (Fig 4, SI XII). (8) Polarization: bipartisan cosponsorship index, lobbyist bipartisan index, modularity (SI XIII).
extraction.scope: US federal lobbying disclosed under the Lobbying Disclosure Act (LDA) of 1995 as amended by HLOGA 2007, years 1999-2023. Population is registrants, clients and lobbyists in LD-2 filings. Excludes informal or unreported advocacy (stated scope condition, SI I.C), PAC and donation channels (only mentioned), LD-203 contribution reports, 'no activity' filings, and superseded filings. Institutions covered: Congress (legislators and committees) and federal agencies and departments.

key_findings.finding: Annual churn of K-Street registrants: 200-500 new registrants enter each year, with a comparable number exiting.
Long-run turnover: of the registrants active in 2000, only a minority remain active in 2020.
key_findings.location: main text p. 5 (cites Fig 2C; survival curve is labeled Fig 2D in caption)

key_findings.finding: Client-registrant rewiring is large: a substantial share of clientship ties is replaced every year.
key_findings.numbers: up to one-third of clientship connections each year

key_findings.finding: Linear preferential attachment: the chance a new client selects a registrant is proportional to that registrant's current client count. Attachment and detachment are both linear in degree and act as countervailing forces.
key_findings.location: main text pp. 4-5 (Fig 2E); SI VIII.B (Fig S27)
key_findings.numbers: cumulative attachment function ~ c^2; quadratic functional form

key_findings.finding: Heavy-tailed clients-per-K-Street-registrant distribution: a small elite dominates the lobbying market.
key_findings.location: main text p. 5 (Fig 2F caption p. 4); SI IV.B (Fig S11)
key_findings.numbers: power-law exponent d = 1.46 (caption) / about 1.5 (text) / 1.54 (SI); cutoff c0 = 86 (caption) / about 85 (text) / 86 (SI)

key_findings.finding: Income concentration among registrants.
key_findings.numbers: about 80% of K-Street income from 20% of registrants

key_findings.finding: Global layer-to-layer degree distributions were stable across 25 years despite high member churn.
Short-term decline in active K-Street firms after 2009, persisting for much of the following decade. Causes are offered as plausible (2007-08 crisis; HLOGA 2007 revolving-door limits) but not tested.
key_findings.numbers: decline after 2009 (no magnitude stated in text)

key_findings.finding: Issue portfolios respond to crises: spikes in disaster-planning and small-business lobbying in early COVID-19; portfolio rearrangement after 9/11 and during COVID-19.
key_findings.numbers: no numeric values given in text

key_findings.finding: Target (agency) portfolios are block-diagonal across presidential terms; lobbyists keep approaching the same agencies within an administration but adapt quickly on leadership change. Some agencies such as the National Economic Council follow the presidential election cycle.
key_findings.location: main text pp. 5-6; Fig 3F; SI XI (Figs S34-S38)
key_findings.numbers: qualitative; PCA: e1 explains more than 48% (text) or 38% (caption) of variance; e2 explains 13%

key_findings.finding: SOPA 2011: IT-sector firms were far more represented among SOPA lobbyists than in the general client base, and IT firms hired multiple K-Street firms, approached the Executive Office of the President more often, and assembled bipartisan lobbying teams more often.
key_findings.location: main text p. 8; Fig 4 (inset Fig 4B; panels C-E); SI XII
key_findings.numbers: P(IT | SOPA) > 0.4 vs P(IT) about 0.1 (shift about +0.3, derived from the stated values); no numeric values stated for panels C-E

key_findings.finding: Monetary concentration of lobbying is persistently high; lobbyist income concentration is lower but above US income Gini.
key_findings.numbers: cumulative Gini about 0.8 for clients and K-Street registrants over 2 decades; about 0.6 for lobbyists; US income Gini about 0.4 (World Bank, as cited)

key_findings.finding: Client-level 80-20 rule for lobbying expenditure.
Registrant-lobbyist contracts are hierarchical at the firm level but egalitarian at the individual lobbyist level.
key_findings.location: SI V.A (Fig S17); SI IV.B (Fig S12C-D); pp. 16, 19
key_findings.numbers: 20% of K-Street registrants hold more than 70% of lobbyist contracts; about 90% of lobbyists have no documented government or legislator association

key_findings.finding: Exit probability of lobbying actors falls with age, with a shared timescale of about 10 years across clients, registrants and lobbyists.
Network-structure checks: clustering coefficients of bipartite projections match the configuration-model null. Only the client-K-Street subgraph has a giant connected component at all times.
key_findings.numbers: qualitative match; no numeric values in text

key_findings.finding: Registrant income is high when a registrant reaches government or legislator associations; each association type alone is sufficient for high income.
key_findings.numbers: qualitative; income in USD by association count

key_findings.finding: Polarization contrast: Senate cosponsorship across parties fell sharply, while lobbying shows no matching trend. Bipartisan lobbying teams earn more income per lobbyist.
key_findings.location: SI XIII (Fig S46); pp. 48-50; main text p. 8 (Fig 4D)
key_findings.numbers: Senate bipartisan cosponsorship down about 40% over 25 years; lobbyist bipartisan index not decreasing; lobbyist modularity near zero

key_findings.finding: Legislator-lobbyist ties via past employment are common but incomplete.
key_findings.location: main text pp. 2-3; SI III (Fig S9); p. 10
key_findings.numbers: 20% of lobbyists had a known government connection in 2023; main text says 80% of Senators and 60% of Representatives have at least one active connected lobbyist, while SI III says about 80% and 50% (inconsistent)

limitations: Revolving-door and legislator ties are inferred only from past-employment disclosures. Lobbyists do not give timelines for covered positions, so recency cannot be established (SI I.D).
Direct registrant-legislator contacts are not required by the LDA and are not observed.

The client-registrant-lobbyist layered graph is a first-order approximation that obscures polyadic interactions; higher-order and multilayer structure is deferred to future work (main pp. 2-3; SI VI; Discussion p. 8).

Entity resolution is imperfect. Client matching uses search-assisted disambiguation, which the paper says fails for long-defunct firms and non-public-facing firms, and resolves to third-party directories (SI I.C fn. 2). Lobbyist name resolution is score-based and uncertain.
Low-cost filings are assigned a reporting-threshold value as an upper bound, a heuristic the paper says is immaterial to results (SI I.C).
Filings for 1999-2007 were on paper and needed OCR, and the 2008 switch from semiannual to quarterly filing doubled report counts; the paper aggregates to annual data.
Only about 40% of clients can be mapped to NAICS sectors via Compustat, so sector-level results cover public or Compustat-linked firms only (SI XII.A).
The SOPA analysis is a single bill, a single quarter, and a restricted subsample; the paper says subsampling can bias results (SI V).

The paper states that fitting a network-evolution model to the lobbying network is beyond its scope (SI VIII). Its preferential-attachment interpretation is descriptive and does not test competing mechanisms.
Polarization analysis is described by the authors as exploratory (SI XIII).

Reported numbers conflict across the text: power-law exponent (1.46 / 1.5 / 1.54); PCA variance (48% vs 38%); legislator connection shares (60% vs 50% for Representatives); survival-curve panel (Fig 2C vs 2D); filing count (1.6 million vs 1,277,411 analyzed).
Anonymized relational data and code are on OSF (osf.io/y2hnm); full identifiers and some fields require contacting the authors (SI XIV).

summary_md:
Bacik, Ondras, Rudkin, Dunkel and Kim build a yearly five-layer directed network from LobbyView, which is derived from LDA LD-2 filings. The layers are clients, registrants (K-Street firms and in-house departments), lobbyists, government entities and legislators. The analyzed sample is 1,277,411 filings from 1999 to 2023. The work is descriptive network physics, not causal inference. Its main findings: 200-500 K-Street registrants enter and leave each year, and only 20% of the firms active in 2000 were still active in 2020. Up to one-third of client-registrant ties are rewired each year. Attachment is linearly preferential, which gives a heavy-tailed distribution of clients per firm (exponent about 1.5, cutoff about 86). Money is concentrated: the cumulative Gini is about 0.8 for clients and firms. Agency-target portfolios form blocks by presidential administration. Senate cross-party cosponsorship fell about 40% while lobbyist bipartisanship did not fall. A single SOPA case (Q4 2011, 67 public firms) shows the IT sector over-represented, with P(IT | SOPA) above 0.4 against a base rate of about 0.1.

For Paul's systems the paper matters mostly through what LDA data cannot show. Legislators enter the paper's network only through lobbyists' one-time disclosures of past covered positions. Those disclosures have no dates, and the LDA never records registrant-legislator contact. That independently supports the system's refutation of the lobbied-member link and its fail-closed handling of contacts and identities. The paper's 40% NAICS coverage supports the rule that client names decide classification. Its K-Street versus in-house distinction supports Mentat's rule of never adding hired-firm and in-house lobbying. Its "election synchronization" finding is about which agencies are targeted, not about money, so it does not support a phase effect on lobbying dollars. The paper contains no press or sentiment data.

bearings.paper_claim: The LDA does not require reporting of direct registrant-legislator contacts, and the paper does not observe them. Legislators enter the network only through a lobbyist's disclosed past covered position: 'legislator inclusion via active lobbyist'. About 90% of lobbyists have no documented government or legislator association, and 20% had a known government connection in 2023.
bearings.paper_location: main pp. 2-3; SI I.D (pp. 20-21); SI III (Fig S9); SI IV.B (Fig S12C-D); SI p. 23
bearings.system_side: The member-year network credits every sponsor and cosponsor of a lobbied bill. That makes P(joined | lobbied) = 1 by construction, so the link is REFUTED as evidence of influence. The interaction ledger states that the LD-2 form has no position field and has no member field.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The evidence carries over fully because it describes the same federal LD-2 form. gaps_exposed: The system has no government-entity (agency or chamber) layer from LD-2. Lobbying links reach Congress only through bill citations. The paper shows agency targeting shifts by administration, and that executive-branch targeting (EOP) separated the IT firms on SOPA.

Lobbying relationships are not treated as time-varying. Up to one-third of client-registrant ties rewire each year and about 20% of registrants survive two decades, so any static organization-to-firm or firm-to-lobbyist mapping goes stale within a year.

There is no configuration-model null for the staffer or cosponsor graphs. The paper tests clustering and giant components against a bipartite configuration model, which would directly test whether staffer degree is container size (r = 0.87 recorded).
Whether the bulk export's post-2021 issue-code collapse is a vintage artifact is unchecked. The paper plots issue portfolios through 2023 and points to OSF data (osf.io/y2hnm). This is UNVERIFIED.
The low-cost-report upper-bound imputation and the 2008 change from semiannual to quarterly filing are not documented as checks in Melange's or Mentat's LDA level series.
flags: Paul's press-pillar and press-value-aggregate positions credit a 'Bacik augmentation' (sentiment-scored press as a determinant of pathway change). The paper contains no press, news-cycle, social or sentiment data. This is Paul's own extension and should not be cited as Bacik's evidence.

Paul's cycle-model position reads Bacik as showing that lobbying synchronizes with the election cycle and that more money flows in election years. The paper's synchronization claim is about which agencies are targeted (blocks by presidential administration), not about dollars, so do not cite it for a phase coefficient on lobbying spend.

The revolving-door figures (80% of Senators and 60% of Representatives in the main text, versus about 80% and 50% in the SI, with at least one connected lobbyist) are inconsistent within the paper. They are past-employment ties with no dates. Never quote them as access or influence (influence language is barred on revolving-door edges, and D-025 applies).

The paper's networks are unweighted and disregard multi-edges by convention (SI pp. 22-23). That is not an argument for per-edge volume normalization or for dropping regular cosponsorship edges, both of which were REJECTED in this project. Do not cite it that way.

Check staffer_routing.py against D-021. It builds person-to-person hops from co-listing on LDA filings ('co_reported_lobbying_activity' at reported_activity_cost 2, and 'co_reported_firm_association' as a weak opt-in at filing_cost 5). It is unconfirmed whether the reported-activity hop is on by default. If it is, LDA is acting as an edge source.
Preferential attachment is descriptive only. The authors say fitting an evolution model is outside their scope, so it should not seed any weight or prior.
SOPA is one bill, one quarter and 67 public firms. P(IT | SOPA) above 0.4 versus about 0.1 has no strata or uncertainty and should be quoted as a single-case illustration.
Any new analysis here that reuses the paper's g and p functions or its bipartisan index on Melange data stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul's markup (217 highlights, no notes) focuses on LobbyView construction, disambiguation, the g and p association functions, registrant types, preferential attachment, election-cycle targeting and the polarization contrast. The parts that bear on the built system agree with it: the system treats LobbyView as an identity source, keeps names decisive over NAICS, keeps in-house and hired-firm spending apart, and borrows only documented definitions for contact inference. The paper's own admission that legislator contact is unobserved strengthens the system's refutation of the lobbied-member link. Paul's cited positions do not record that refutation, so they are stale on that point. Two of Paul's positions over-read the paper. The 'Bacik augmentation' with press sentiment is not in the paper, and the election-cycle synchronization concerns agency targets, not money. His readings for cooperation-v2 and bpf come from the lobbyist bipartisan index, which classifies agents and is not a member-level cooperation trait. The paper does document that the Senate cross-party cosponsorship baseline fell about 40%, which argues for naming the window on bpf.

Kim and Kunisky build bipartite lobbying networks from the same LobbyView and LDA bill links. They give the community-structure counterpart to Bacik's time evolution.
It adds LLM-coded bill positions to LobbyView reports. That fills the position field LD-2 lacks, which Bacik's network also lacks.
It takes the hypergraph and higher-order approach that Bacik defers to future work, applied to the EU lobby network.
Bacik cites it (ref 1) as the survey of empirical lobbying models that the descriptive network work sits beside.
It studies the partisan ties of lobbying firms, which bears on Bacik's finding that lobbying is bipartisan and not polarized.

meta.title: Empirical Models of Lobbying
meta.venue: Annual Review of Economics 12:391-413 (first published online May 13, 2020)

extraction.title: Empirical Models of Lobbying
extraction.venue: Annual Review of Economics 12:391-413 (first published online May 13, 2020)
extraction.document_type: Review article (narrative literature review; no original estimation or sample). Metadata hint verified against the PDF front matter; no correction needed.
extraction.coverage: Full text read in full (text file lines 1-1170, covering journal pp. 391-413 including the literature cited list). Annotation file read in full: 106 highlights, zero sticky notes, so no note text exists. Page numbers in the annotation file are PDF page indices (PDF page n corresponds to journal page n+390).
extraction.research_question: Is lobbying (direct or intermediated business-government interaction over policy) welfare-enhancing or welfare-distorting? The review organizes recent empirical work on quid pro quo and informational lobbying, asks how to identify policy supply and demand and the counterfactual equilibrium with no lobbying, and assesses how distorted equilibrium policy is relative to the social optimum.
extraction.theory: Quid pro quo perspective: Grossman and Helpman (1994, 1996) menu-auction and electoral models; policy supply and demand framework (lD = C Q^(1-1/eps), lS = G Q^(1+1/eta)), Figure 1; Tullock (1967) contest function as used by Kang (2016); bargaining across heterogeneous special interests (Bombardini and Trebbi 2011). Informational perspective: cheap talk (Crawford and Sobel 1982; Krishna and Morgan 2001; Battaglini 2002), costly or money-burning signaling (Potters and van Winden 1992; Grossman and Helpman 2001), hybrid access-fee models (Austen-Smith 1995; Lohmann 1995), legislative subsidy (Hall and Deardorff 2006), and information verification by lobbying intermediaries (Groll and Ellis 2014; Hirsch et al. 2019).
extraction.data: No original data. Sources surveyed: LDA filings via Senate Office of Public Records (SOPR) and CRP (total lobbying about $3-3.5 billion per year over the decade to 2019 versus $200-250 million PAC donations; average 12,537 unique lobbyists per year 1998-2019, 11,654 in 2018; about 37,000 active lobbyists 1999-2008 per Bertrand et al. 2014); FEC and CRP PAC data; LobbyView/Compustat (Huneeus and Kim 2019: 766 of 7,646 US public firms lobbied in 2017); Washington Representatives directory (about 14,000 of 37,000 lobbyists profiled); LegiStorm staffer salaries (2012); Kang (2016) 538 energy policies in 445 bills, 110th Congress; Hirsch et al. (2019) 219 FARA lobbyists, 110th-111th Congress; federal rulemaking comments from 150 agencies (Bertrand et al. 2018a); Canada Registry (about 9,000 lobbyists, 2017-18); EU Transparency Register (5,431 registrants in 2012, 11,901 in 2018).
extraction.method: Narrative review organized as quid pro quo (structural econometric and reduced-form) versus informational. Structural methods reviewed: Kang (2016) Tullock-contest game with simulated maximum likelihood and equilibrium selection; Bombardini and Trebbi (2011) structural first-order conditions yielding a dollar-per-vote cost; Huneeus and Kim (2019) heterogeneous-firm general-equilibrium model estimated by minimum distance on simulated moments. Reduced-form methods reviewed: difference-in-differences (Blanes i Vidal et al. 2012), instrumental variables (de Figueiredo and Silverman 2006 with overhead rates; Goldstein and You 2017 with distance to Washington), natural experiments (Kerr et al. 2014 H-1B cap; Dellavigna et al. 2016 Berlusconi advertising), and observational contact and mobility regressions (Bertrand et al. 2014; Hirsch et al. 2019). Text methods: NLP to classify bill policies (Kang 2016, p.397) and latent semantic analysis of comments (Bertrand et al. 2018a, p.408, n.35).
extraction.identification: Varies by paper. Huneeus and Kim (2019): committee-assignment shocks to senators connected to firms (p.401, n.18). Kang (2016): equilibrium selection (maximizes sum of payoffs) and simulated counterfactual with no lobbying. de Figueiredo and Silverman (2006): university overhead rates shift policy demand (p.403). Goldstein and You (2017): political mismatch between city and state, with distance from Washington as IV (p.403, n.20). Kerr et al. (2014): predetermined H-1B cap expiry, differential exposure (p.404). Blanes i Vidal et al. (2012): exit of connected senator, assumed exogenous (p.404). Dellavigna et al. (2016): Berlusconi office-holding shifts ad spending to Mediaset (p.405-406). Bertrand et al. (2014): committee reassignment of politicians and lobbyist following (p.405).
extraction.scope: Population: mainly US federal lobbying (LDA data 1999-2019 with 1998 onward totals), public and business interests, mostly the Congress and federal agencies; secondary sections on Canada (Sec. 5.1) and EU (Sec. 5.2). Institutions: Congress, federal agencies, Senate and House committees, and EU Commission and Parliament. Era: literature from the 1990s through 2019, with some references to 1971 FECA disclosure rules and the 2007 LDA amendments.

key_findings.finding: Survey context: 53% of respondents called lobbyists and special interest groups in Washington a very big problem, versus 38% for illegal immigration (Pew surveys, Sept 2018-Mar 2019).
Kang (2016) energy-sector lobbying: only 8% of 538 policies in 445 bills are enacted; policies with no lobbying are enacted about 1% of the time; policies with two or more lobbying players about 24%.
key_findings.numbers: 8% overall; 1% no lobbying; 24% two or more lobbyists

key_findings.finding: Kang's model implies lobbying raises enactment by only 0.021% to 0.415% over an 8% baseline, and average returns to lobbying of 137% (renewables) to 152% (oil and gas). The implied monetary value per policy above $500 million is flagged by the authors as possibly signaling misspecification.

Bombardini and Trebbi (2011) structural bargaining model on Congressional campaign contributions estimates $200-$400 of donations per vote acquired and a precise average rate of return on political spending. Adding the electoral-vote channel makes implied returns far more reasonable.
key_findings.numbers: $200-$400 per vote; agriculture return about $13.7 per dollar at the margin; simulated returns 10%-20% per year

key_findings.finding: Farm Bill comparison: about $22 billion in 2000 agribusiness subsidies against under $3.7 million in agribusiness PAC contributions implies a naive return of about 600,000%, which the authors argue shows that observable contributions miss other influence channels.

Huneeus and Kim (2019): a 10% increase in lobbying raises revenue 3%. Federal lobbying reduces aggregate US productivity 22%, with 59% from misallocation to lobbying (less productive) firms and 41% from missing entry of productive firms.

Huneeus and Kim lobbying facts: 766 of 7,646 US public firms lobbied in 2017; lobbying firms have about four times the revenue of non-lobbying firms; elasticity of lobbying to sales about one conditional on lobbying.
Lobbying is persistent: 92% of firms that lobby in a year also lobby the next year (Kerr et al. 2014), consistent with large sunk entry costs.

Industry-association share: individual firms account for an average 67% (median 96%) of lobbying per Bombardini and Trebbi (2012), and industries with lower concentration and differentiation use trade associations more.

Scale of federal lobbying: total spending about $3-3.5 billion per year over the decade, versus $200-250 million per year in PAC donations; about 12,537 unique lobbyists per year 1998-2019 on average.

Earmarks (de Figueiredo and Silverman 2006): an extra dollar of lobbying yields about one dollar more in earmarks for universities with no Appropriations-committee ties, and $4.52-$5.24 for universities with connections.
Goldstein and You (2017) cities: approximate return of $1.02 in earmarks and $0.47 in 2009 Recovery Act grants per $1 of lobbying, using distance-based IV.

Kerr et al. (2014): after the H-1B visa cap reduction, high-skill-immigration lobbying as a share of total lobbying doubles for dependent firms; the effect is stronger for firms that lobbied on other issues before, consistent with fixed entry costs.

Blanes i Vidal et al. (2012): revolving-door lobbyists (former aides) lose a persistent 24% of lobbying revenue when their connected senator exits office. Drops are larger for Finance, Appropriations, or Ways and Means connections and insignificant otherwise; the exit-exogeneity assumption is flagged as strong.

Bertrand et al. (2014): about 37,000 active lobbyists in 1999-2008; in-house share fell from nearly 60% to under 40%; external lobbying doubled 1999-2008. Lobbyists follow politicians across committees, and the expertise premium does not rise with issue relevance, which the authors read as access dominating expertise.
key_findings.numbers: about 37,000 lobbyists; in-house share 60% to <40%; external lobbying doubled

key_findings.finding: Dellavigna et al. (2016): regulated firms in Italy shift advertising onto Berlusconi-owned Mediaset during his periods in office, only in heavily regulated industries, at a scale of hundreds of millions of euros.

Hirsch et al. (2019) FARA data: lobbying contact is more likely with ideologically aligned Members, and conditional on contact, lobbyists with ideological closeness or prior connections bring fewer clients and set higher certification thresholds.
Bertrand et al. (2018a) with latent semantic analysis of rulemaking comments from 150 agencies: a nonprofit comment's similarity to its benefactor's comments rises immediately after a donation.

Canada: about 9,000 registered lobbyists in 2017-18, just over 1,000 external; compared with 11,654 US lobbyists in the same year. Hickey (2014) finds only 6% of Canadian lobbyists follow reshuffled ministers.

EU: the voluntary Transparency Register grew from 5,431 registrants (2012) to 11,901 (2018). Apple reported EUR 2-2.25 million of EU lobbying in 2018 versus $6.7 million in the US. Dellis and Sondermann (2017) match about 2,000 Orbis firms to the register.

limitations: Authors state that the two main unresolved issues are how to account for lobbying's effect on which equilibrium policies are chosen, and how distorted those policies are relative to the social optimum (abstract, p.391); a comprehensive welfare assessment is described as elusive.
Authors caution that the review resolves little of the good-or-bad question (Sec. 1, p.392).
Lobbying may be invisible to researchers when it blocks change, leaving only a status quo with no visible law change (p.393).

Informational models are rare in empirical work because data on the informational needs of agents and on transmitted expertise are very hard to obtain (p.394). Information is hard to quantify (p.393).

Structural models show signs of misspecification: Kang's near-zero lobbying effect and $500m+ implied value per policy (pp.398-399); the authors say some structural models display symptoms of misspecification (p.410).
Structural identification is not assured: Huneeus and Kim's minimum-distance criterion may not have a unique minimizer and should be probed with Monte Carlo (p.401).
Kang (2016) equilibrium multiplicity: equilibrium is selected by maximizing total payoffs; budget constraints are excluded and games treated as independent (p.398, n.14).

Exogeneity and exclusion assumptions: Blanes i Vidal et al. assume senator exit is orthogonal to lobbyist fortunes, which is strong if senators retire strategically (p.404); distance IV in Goldstein and You is open to exclusion-restriction criticism (p.403, n.20); Goldstein and You do not use cumulative transfers (p.403, n.21).

Measurement of lobbying effects: Kang's policy-level and bill-level mapping needed heavy preprocessing; omitting bill refinement would mismeasure lobbying effects (p.398, n.12). Lobbying spending alone is not the full influence arsenal (Sec. 2, p.394).

Cross-country comparability limited: Canadian Registry lacks fee data (p.409); EU register is voluntary with limited history, and EU firm counts are not directly comparable with Compustat counts (p.410).

summary_md:
Bombardini and Trebbi (2020) is a narrative review of empirical lobbying research. It contains no new estimation. It sorts the literature into quid pro quo models, where political resources are exchanged for policy, and informational models, where interest groups pass expertise to less-informed policymakers. It then asks how each line of work identifies policy supply and demand and the counterfactual of no lobbying.

The review reaches three conclusions that matter for Paul's systems.

First, structural estimates of what money buys are fragile. Kang (2016) estimates that lobbying raises enactment by only 0.021% to 0.415% over an 8% baseline (538 energy policies, 110th Congress), yet the same model implies more than $500m of value per policy. A naive Farm Bill comparison gives a return near 600,000% ($22bn of 2000 subsidies against under $3.7m of agribusiness PAC money). The authors read these figures as symptoms of misspecification or of influence channels left out of the model. Adding an electoral-vote channel (Bombardini and Trebbi 2011) brings implied returns down to plausible levels.

Second, lobbying is persistent: 92% of firms that lobby in one year lobby the next (Kerr et al. 2014). The structure of the industry has also shifted: from 1999 to 2008 the in-house share of lobbying fell from about 60% to under 40%, while external lobbying doubled.

Third, in the revolving-door literature, a lobbyist's revenue depends on the patron staying in office. Former aides lose a persistent 24% of revenue when their senator exits (Blanes i Vidal et al. 2012), and lobbyists follow politicians across committee reassignments (Bertrand et al. 2014).

For the system as built, the review supports keeping money a minority, saturating channel in the flip and money-response engines, and treating ROI figures as fragile. It supports the persistence-based lobbying nowcast in Mentat and the rule that in-house and outside-firm lobbying are never summed. It also exposes one gap: the staffer route costs decay with time since overlap but do not account for whether the anchoring member is still in office or holds a powerful committee seat.

gaps_exposed: Staffer and revolving-door routing has no term for whether the anchoring member is still in office or sits on a high-stakes committee (Finance, Appropriations, Ways and Means). The review's strongest revolving-door evidence ties a connection's revenue value to exactly those facts, while the system models only time decay since overlap.

There is no independent contact measure for lobbying. LD-2 filings never name members, and the review's contact-level evidence comes from FARA (Hirsch et al.), whose coverage excludes the domestic CU and bank clients this system tracks.

The planned contested-bill counterparty term has no functional form. The review's main structural template (a Tullock contest between opposing coalitions) relies on equilibrium selection and shows misspecification symptoms.

The system has no informational channel. Every money and lobbying lever is quid pro quo or pressure, while the review treats the informational view (cheap talk, legislative subsidy, opposing-bias senders) as one of the two main families.
No owner-ratified mechanism checks ROI and break-even outputs for plausibility. The review shows returns computed from observable contributions are routinely implausible.
flags: D-104..D-108: the review does not validate the competitiveness reciprocity premise. Bombardini and Trebbi (2011) has an electoral-vote channel via persuadable voters, but it does not estimate that dollars buy more in competitive seats. Do not cite this paper for COMPET_MULT.

Revolving-door wording rule: Blanes i Vidal's 24% figure is a revenue loss for former aides turned lobbyists. Any use in staffer routing must avoid influence or access language, and under D-025 it must not be treated as an introduction probability.
D-021: a Kang-style contest weighted by LDA spend would use LDA as a weight source. A contested-bills extension built that way needs an owner ruling first.

Kang's descriptive enactment rates (1% with no lobbying vs 24% with two or more lobbying players) carry selection bias and are not a lobbying effect. The review's own structural estimate is 0.021%-0.415%.
The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). Nothing to flag on those.
paul_alignment: Paul recorded no takeaway for this paper; both annotation entries are empty. Measured against his positions on other components, the review backs the system's conservative stance over his ROI enthusiasm. It shows that contribution-based returns are routinely implausible, which is consistent with his calling the Alexander figure an outlier, and it supports keeping money a minority channel in the flip model. It also reports the Huneeus and Kim committee-assignment instrument he cites for the committee pillar. extraction.method: Descriptive data engineering in Python 3.6.4: ElementTree parses the XML hierarchy; os.listdir enumerates files; a parsing loop (pseudocode in Fig. 2) converts records into Pandas data frames, with defaultdict holding a master dictionary (Sec. 2.2-2.3). Filing and Issue frames are merged, and reported dollar amounts are summed by issue code (a Pandas series grouped by code, Sec. 2.3). A search function returns every record whose Specific Issues text contains a user-supplied term; the term "pediatric" is used (Sec. 2.4). Search hits are compared with the code-level totals (Sec. 2.4). No statistical tests, models or regressions are run.
extraction.scope: Population: lobbying disclosures filed under the LDA in one calendar quarter (Q4 2009), covering all issue areas, with a pediatric subset identified by keyword. Institution: US federal Congress and federal agencies (the LDA). Era: pre-ACA (2009-2010 passage). A single-quarter, single-keyword methods illustration, not a population-level or multi-year study.

summary_md:
Harrison, Dreisbach, Basit and Keim-Malpass (2018) is a short data report, not a study of influence. It parses one quarter of Senate LDA XML (Q4 2009, just before the ACA) into eight pandas data frames. It sums reported dollars by umbrella issue code (Taxation $527.1M, Health $436.7M, with no denominator for the filing count) and finds 35 records whose Specific Issues text contains "pediatric". It runs no statistics. Its useful content is a list of data hazards:
- **Two series mixed:** the XML amount field does not separate in-house expenditures from outside-firm income.
- **Imprecise amounts:** expenses under $5,000 appear only as a checkbox, and income is rounded to the nearest $10,000.
- **Bundled issues:** one filing lists many issues, so dollars cannot be assigned to a single issue.
- **Filing time vs activity time:** files are grouped by when they were filed, so a quarter's files can carry activity from 2002 to 2008.

For Paul's systems, those hazards matter more than the results. Mentat's lobbying card and `sector_spend.py` now enforce the paper's main warning. They keep outside-firm fees and in-house expenses as two series and never add them (D-064, commit 914623152, which removed a double-counted $139.4M telecom total on 2026-10-09). `sector_spend.py` also assigns filings by activity period and keeps only the latest amendment.

The older LobbyView collector does not follow the same rule. Its per-side `amount_sum` and its top-spender `total_amount` add self-filer expenses and hired-firm income together. The brain's "ABA $228M vs CUNA $93M" figure probably comes from that mixed sum (UNVERIFIED). On issue codes, the collector correctly counts reports rather than dollars, which avoids the bundling trap that inflates the paper's own per-code dollar totals. The paper has nothing to say about networks, persuasion, legislators or elections.

bearings.paper_claim: LDA amount fields do not separate lobbying expenditures (in-house) from income (outside-firm fees), and nothing in the record links the two. Expenses under $5,000 are a checkbox with no amount, and income over $5,000 is rounded to the nearest $10,000. Reported dollars therefore cannot be split by type, and small spenders show no amount.
bearings.system_side: The LobbyView collector reads is_self_filer for each report. Its per-side, per-year amount_sum and finance_amount_sum, and its top-spender total_amount, still add every report's amount, whether self-filer expense or hired-firm income. Self-filer dollars are kept only as a sub-sum. Blank amounts are parsed as 0.0. The brain note records 'ABA $228M vs CUNA $93M' and 'self-filer = expense, hired firm = gross income'. A self-filer's expense figure already includes its payments to outside firms, so adding the outside firms' income for the same client counts those dollars twice. This is the double count that D-064 bans in sector_spend.py.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The hazard carries over directly: the LD-2 form semantics the paper describes still hold in the LobbyView vintage (2024-10-25). The paper's claim that the XML cannot separate the two series does not carry over: LobbyView exposes is_self_filer, so the system can split them and simply does not in these aggregates. Window: LobbyView reports for 1999-2024, with finance-joined coverage reliable through 2021. Two points are UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062): whether the brain's $228M ABA figure is the mixed total_amount, and how large the overlap is.

gaps_exposed: The LobbyView collector's spend aggregates (amount_sum, finance_amount_sum, top-spender total_amount) add self-filer expenses and hired-firm income. This contradicts the D-064 rule that sector_spend.py and Mentat now enforce. The ABA $228M vs CUNA $93M comparison in the brain may be a mixed figure. It should be re-derived as two separate series before it is quoted again.

Amounts reported only as the under-$5,000 checkbox are parsed as 0.0 in the LobbyView ingest, and income above $5,000 is rounded to the nearest $10,000. No receipt counts how many finance-side reports are affected. Small credit-union filers such as state leagues would be understated relative to large bank filers.

Neither Melange nor Mentat uses the Specific Issues free text. The paper proposes NLP and topic modeling on it as future work, and Kim et al. 2025 do the position-extraction version. The system's issue view is limited to issue codes and report counts.
flags: Do not quote the paper's per-code dollar totals (Taxation $527.1M, Health $436.7M) as benchmarks. They come from a Filing x Issue merge that probably counts a multi-issue filing's dollars under every code, they mix expenditure and income, and the paper gives no filing-count denominator.

Paul's positions list cites Harrison for mentat-fec-attribution.dedup-and-versions ('late-filed records'). The paper is about LDA filing-time vs activity-time grouping and says nothing about FEC amendment or memo versions, so the citation does not carry over to that component. The LDA analogue is already handled in sector_spend.py (activity-period assignment plus latest-dt_posted supersession).
Paul's positions list also cites Harrison for melange-legislative-data.congress-activity-score. The paper does not touch congress.gov bill data, so it has no bearing on that component.
The paper uses LDA dollars only as spend totals and builds no edges, so it raises no D-021 conflict. Any future reuse must keep LDA as an identity source, not an edge or weight source.
paul_alignment: The evidence agrees with Paul's takeaway: the paper is an introductory walkthrough of an LDA pipeline (pandas, where to get the records, how to turn them into usable information), and its results are thin, with one quarter, one keyword and no statistics. His note that Kim's LobbyView is far larger also holds, and the system uses LobbyView as its historical source. His note misses where the paper's real value lies. Its stated limits (expenditures and income not separated, the under-$5,000 checkbox, $10,000 rounding, issue bundling, filing-time grouping) are the hazards the system has since ruled on: D-064 says never add the two series, D-130 sets the deadline-based quarter coverage rule, and the 10-09 commit removed the summed telecom figure. In that sense his note is out of date. It treats the paper as a how-to; the system now follows its warnings in Mentat and sector_spend.py but not yet in the LobbyView collector's spend aggregates.

extraction.title: The partisan ties of lobbying firms
extraction.venue: Research & Politics, July-September 2019, pp. 1-9 (volume and issue not stated in the extracted text)
extraction.document_type: Peer-reviewed journal article; empirical quantitative study (open access, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 1,151 lines of the extracted text file (front matter, abstract, introduction, theory, research design, descriptive statistics, Tables 1-3, difference-in-differences results, conclusion, acknowledgements, funding, references). Figures 1-4 are covered through captions and surrounding text only. Online Appendices A-G and replication files are cited but not in the extracted text, so their contents are not covered. Paul's markup: the single annotation file was read; it holds 24 highlights, all with empty note text. Metadata hint corrected: the hint left authors blank (three authors now listed); title, year, venue and DOI in the hint were confirmed.
extraction.research_question: Do partisan ties between US lobbying firms and the partisan leadership of Congress raise the revenue those firms earn from clients? Are lobbying firms institutions with relatively stable partisan identities, and do ties to House and Senate majorities return different amounts (abstract; pp.1-2)?
extraction.theory: A partisan theory of legislative subsidy. Legislators have scarce time and staff and gain from lobbyists' information, intelligence and labor (Hall and Deardorff 2006). Legislators trust their closest allies, and in a polarized era allies are mostly co-partisans, so a firm's partisan organizational identity signals that it is an ally (p.2). Majority status gives access that outside interests pay more for (Cox and Magar 1999), so co-partisanship with the chamber majority should raise client payments (p.2). H1: firms with partisan ties to the majority party earn more than firms without such ties. H2: partisan ties to the House majority return more than ties to the Senate majority, plausibly because Senate staffing is larger per member, so clients pay less for Senate lobbying (pp.2-3). Baker (2008) interviews add a second account: lobbyists view senators as harder to lobby (cross-pressured, broad-interest, less attentive to detail) (p.3). Firm-level controls (client count, client diversity, law-firm status, international offices, domestic offices, age) are expected to shape prestige, risk spreading and scale economies (p.3).
extraction.identification: Two strategies. (1) Panel regressions with firm random effects and year fixed effects; the authors note Senate effects may be suppressed by multicollinearity (Online Appendix C, not in extracted text). (2) First differences (Change in revenue on change in X), which removes residual unobserved firm heterogeneity and time-invariant covariates (p.6). For causation, the authors treat changes in chamber control as exogenous interventions: the 2011 House takeover by Republicans (Tea Party period) and the 2015 Senate takeover by Republicans. They use kernel-weighted difference-in-differences (Hazlett 2019) comparing firms aligned with the party gaining control against firms aligned with the ousted party (p.7). Argument: firms would not be newly founded as in-party firms right after a takeover, so year-over-year changes are attributed to perceived in-party value; switching of lobbyists between opposite-party firms is said to be ruled out in Online Appendix F (not in extracted text). The text reports no explicit parallel-trends check in the main text.
extraction.data: Unbalanced quarterly panel of 1,603 lobbying firms, Q1 2008 to Q3 2016 (unit: firm-quarter; N = 33,243; T = 2 to 35 quarters per firm; Table 2). Sources: public Lobbying Disclosure Act (LDA) reports (reporting became quarterly after HLOGA 2007); campaign contributions by each firm's lobbyists back to 1990; firm websites for law-firm status (2015), international office (2015), number of domestic offices and firm age. Website covariates are missing for firms without sites (smaller, newer and disbanded firms most at risk) and were multiply imputed (King et al. 2001; Online Appendix A). Sample rule: registrant differs from client (contract lobbyist); at least two active lobbyists in the same quarter at least once; at least two quarters with nonzero dollars. About 84% of firms had nonzero campaign giving (p.4). Dependent variable: revenue per lobbyist per quarter, in real dollars (CPI-U). Table 1: mean US$74,007 (SD 71,481), median US$54,365, range US$776 to US$913,800. Replication data: Harvard Dataverse doi:10.7910/DVN/3HDSM8.
extraction.method: Two sets of linear panel models. Set 1 (levels, Table 2, models 1.1-1.6): revenue per lobbyist regressed on House alignment and Senate alignment, crossed as time-fixed vs time-varying partisanship and 85%, 90% and 95% giving thresholds, plus controls (number of clients, client diversity = Simpson reciprocal diversity of issues plus industries, law firm, international office, domestic offices, firm age). Firm random effects, year fixed effects, HC3 Arellano standard errors clustered by firm. H2 tested with a restricted F-test that the House and Senate coefficients are equal. Set 2 (first differences, Table 3, models 2.1-2.6): change in revenue on change in alignment, clients and diversity. Partisan measure: a firm is aligned with a chamber's leadership party if its lobbyists' contributions exceed the threshold share to that party; bipartisan or unclear firms are coded as aligned with neither chamber (p.3). Reliability: Fleiss kappa 0.86 (time-fixed) and 0.84 (time-varying). Validity: correlations of 0.31 to 0.55 between contribution-based partisanship and founder-based partisanship (web pages); time-fixed vs time-varying correlation 0.62 to 0.63 (p.3). Causal test: kernel-weighted difference-in-differences (Hazlett 2019) around the 2011 and 2015 takeovers (p.7-8).
extraction.scope: US federal contract lobbying firms (registrants that act as contract lobbyists for clients) that meet the LDA sample rules, reporting 2008-2016, after the 2007 HLOGA quarterly-reporting change. Institutions: the House and Senate party leadership. Not a census of all lobbying firms or of in-house lobbying; the 1,603 firms are the sample that met the rules. Individual lobbyists are not the unit of analysis; the firm is (p.1-2, p.8).
measures: Revenue per Lobbyist per Quarter (dependent; real US$, CPI-U adjusted; sum of client income divided by lobbyists)
Firm Partisan Alignment with House Leadership (binary; 1 if the firm's partisan identity matches House leadership)
Firm Partisan Alignment with Senate Leadership (binary; same logic for Senate leadership)
Partisan threshold: 85%, 90% or 95% of lobbyists' contributions to one party
Time-fixed partisan identity (based on contributions dating to 1990) vs time-varying identity (updated yearly from roster and giving)
Number of Clients (unique entities lobbied for; mean 10.36, median 4, max 276)
Client Diversity (Simpson reciprocal index for issues and industries, summed; mean 9.25)
Law Firm, International Office (2015 status, websites); Number of Domestic Offices; Firm Age (observed year minus founding year; mean 18.31)
Founder-based partisanship (for validity check; Democratic, Republican or bipartisan founders)
Change-in-variables versions of all of the above for first-difference models
Takeover treatment indicator for difference-in-differences (aligned with gaining party vs ousted party)

key_findings.finding: Partisan identities of lobbying firms are relatively stable and reliable (kappa and time-fixed/time-varying correlation); founder-based partisanship correlates with contribution-based partisanship.
key_findings.numbers: Fleiss kappa 0.86 time-fixed, 0.84 time-varying; correlations 0.62-0.63 across measures; founder correlations 0.31-0.55 (p<=0.05)

key_findings.finding: Roughly 42-60% of firms are partisan and 40-58% bipartisan, depending on the cutoff; the share distribution is bimodal, with a drop-off after the 95% threshold.
key_findings.numbers: 42-60% partisan; 40-58% bipartisan; 84% of firms had nonzero giving

key_findings.finding: Bipartisan firms consistently earned more average revenue than partisan-leaning firms; Democratic and Republican firms were at rough parity, with a small advantage that shifted with congressional control; unclassified firms earned least.
key_findings.numbers: No point estimates in text; Democratic firms led 2008-2010, Republican firms 2011-2016

key_findings.finding: House partisan alignment is significantly and positively associated with firm revenue in all six panel models (H1 supported for the House).
key_findings.numbers: Time-fixed coefficients 5,536 (SE 1,734), 6,527 (1,944), 6,096 (2,132); time-varying 5,148 (1,298), 5,346 (1,343), 4,940 (1,396); all p<=0.05. Text: about US$5,000-6,000 per lobbyist per quarter

key_findings.finding: Senate partisan alignment is significant only with the time-fixed measure, and not with the time-varying measure, so H1 for the Senate is specification-dependent.
The restricted test of equal House and Senate effects (H2) is significant only with time-varying measures.
Changes in House alignment are associated with changes in revenue (first differences); H1 holds for the House in five of six models, with one model just short of conventional significance.
key_findings.numbers: Time-fixed change coefficients 3,520*, 3,638*, 5,048*; time-varying 1,819*, 1,741 (p~0.07), 2,370*; text range US$1,800-5,000 per lobbyist per quarter. No Senate support in first differences

key_findings.finding: Partisan ties to the House are more revenue-enhancing than Senate ties in only two of six first-difference models.
key_findings.numbers: Restricted F significant in models 2.4 (4*) and 2.6 (4*); others 1-3, not significant

key_findings.finding: Controls: number of clients is positive and significant; client diversity is positive and significant in levels but not in first differences; law firm status is strongly negative; international office, domestic offices and firm age are mostly not significant.
key_findings.numbers: Number of Clients about 1,650 per lobbyist per quarter (significant); Client Diversity about 1,310 (significant); Law Firm -5,529* to -6,172* (significant); Change in Client Diversity not significant

key_findings.finding: When Republicans regained the House in 2011, Republican-aligned firms gained and Democratic-aligned firms lost revenue (difference-in-differences; the strongest causal evidence in the paper).
key_findings.location: p.7-8 (Figure 3; text on Tea Party-era takeover)
key_findings.numbers: Republican-aligned firms gained just over US$10,000 for the year; ousted Democratic-aligned firms lost more than US$40,000 in annual revenue, despite the Democrats keeping the Senate

key_findings.finding: The 2015 Republican takeover of the Senate produced no significant revenue effects in the difference-in-differences design.
key_findings.location: p.8 (Figure 4; Online Appendix G for details)
key_findings.numbers: No significant effects reported in text; figure values not in extracted text

key_findings.finding: Tally across tests: House ties support the revenue hypothesis in 12 of 13 tests; Senate ties in only 3 of 13; House-over-Senate advantage in 5 of 12 tests.

Authors' interpretation: partisan ties with the House are a more reliable revenue source than Senate ties, possibly reflecting staffing differences; alternative explanations (longer electoral cycle, supermajority rules, member prominence in the Senate) are not tested. Moosbrugger (2012) suggested as a starting point.

limitations: Senate evidence is mixed and depends on model specification (time-fixed vs time-varying; threshold); the authors say support for H1 for the Senate would be somewhat higher if multicollinearity in models 1.4-1.6 were considered (p.8; Online Appendix C).
The House-over-Senate difference is attributed to staffing differences, but the authors name untested alternatives (electoral cycle, supermajority rules, member prominence) (p.8).
Firm characteristics from websites are missing for firms without sites; smaller, newer and disbanded firms are most at risk; missing values are multiply imputed (p.3, p.5).
The partisan boundary (partisan vs bipartisan) is acknowledged as fuzzy; the authors therefore use three cutoffs and two measures (p.3).
Founder-based validation is a correlation check on the contribution-based measure, not an independent causal test (p.3).
Model 2.5 (time-varying, 85% threshold, first differences) falls just short of conventional significance (p.6).

Difference-in-differences rests on two takeover episodes (2011 House, 2015 Senate); the 2015 Senate test shows no effect. The main text does not report a parallel-trends diagnostic; the authors point to Online Appendix G and to Hazlett (2019) for the estimator.
The 2019 lobbying data were not yet available; the authors plan to re-test after the 2018 midterm switch of House control (p.8).
Causal claims rely on the argument that firms are not newly formed as in-party firms right after a takeover (p.7); the paper states this as a plausibility argument.

summary_md:
Furnas, Heaney and LaPira (2019) ask whether US contract lobbying firms have stable partisan identities and whether ties to the majority party raise their revenue. The sample is 1,603 LDA contract registrants observed by quarter from 2008 Q1 to 2016 Q3 (33,243 firm-quarters). A firm's partisanship comes from the share of its lobbyists' FEC contributions that go to one party, using cutoffs of 85, 90 or 95%. These identities are reliable (Fleiss kappa 0.84 to 0.86). Between 42% and 60% of firms are partisan, and bipartisan firms earn the highest average revenue.

The outcome is real revenue per lobbyist per quarter, with a mean of $74k. In all six levels models, alignment with the House majority adds about $5,000 to $6,000 per lobbyist per quarter. Senate alignment matters only under the time-fixed measure. A kernel-weighted difference-in-differences around the 2011 House flip finds that Republican-aligned firms gained just over $10k over the year while Democratic-aligned firms lost more than $40k. The 2015 Senate flip shows no significant effect. Across all tests, House ties support the revenue hypothesis in 12 of 13 and Senate ties in 3 of 13.

For Paul's systems, the main relevance is to the Mentat sector-growth and lobbying-forecast lanes, not to the Melange engine. The study supports keeping House and Senate separate and expecting a weaker Senate signal. It measures a premium clients are willing to pay for perceived access to the majority. That is a market valuation: it is not a measure of persuasion and not an access probability. The effect is also distributional: control changes move revenue between partisan firms. The paper does not estimate how sector totals respond, which is the level Mentat's lobbying model works at. This reading is UNVERIFIED agent analysis until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: House-majority ties raise contract-firm revenue in 12 of 13 tests; Senate ties in only 3 of 13. In the 2011 House-flip difference-in-differences, Republican-aligned firms gained just over $10k and ousted Democratic-aligned firms lost more than $40k in annual revenue. Both figures are firm-level, one-year windows, on a revenue-per-lobbyist outcome. The 2015 Senate flip shows no significant effect.
bearings.system_side: SEATS-W keeps House and Senate on separate seat scales (sgs_seats.R:24). The brain records one election, the 2022 House, over 17 weeks: -3.47 pp in the Democratic share of giving per +1 expected Democratic seat (block bootstrap p .0086 to .0174), with the Senate null. The result is EXPLORATORY.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The House-yes, Senate-null pattern in SEATS-W matches the paper's House-over-Senate pattern, which supports keeping chamber-specific estimates. The paper does not predict SEATS-W's sign. It measures contract-lobbying revenue after control has actually changed, by firm partisanship. SEATS-W measures the partisan share of PAC and individual giving as within-cycle seat forecasts move. A party-share drop as expected Democratic seats rise is not explained by majority-access pricing, so the paper cannot be cited as evidence for access-seeking in SEATS-W. Both are single-episode designs: one House flip in the paper, one election in SEATS-W.

In 2011, Republican-aligned firms gained about $10k and Democratic-aligned firms lost more than $40k per lobbyist over the year (firm-level difference-in-differences). Democratic firms led in revenue in 2008-2010 and Republican firms in 2011-2016. Bipartisan firms earned the most throughout.

The effect is distributional across firm partisanship. The paper does not identify a sector-total change. A common control shock would be absorbed by factor(year) in the fit, but the forecast cannot include it for future years. Before adding a control-flip term, test whether outside-firm totals step after the 2011, 2015 and 2019 flips. The 2008-2016 era and the HLOGA quarterly regime both apply to the LDA series.

bearings.paper_claim: Majority status carries a revenue premium in the contract-lobbying market of about $5,000 to $6,000 per lobbyist per quarter for House alignment (levels models). The Senate premium depends on specification.
bearings.system_side: The SHIFT tables regress the Republican share of giving on the expected-minus-current control shift. The brain records no stable partisan shift, chamber-stacked: -0.04, p .76. The House estimate is SATURATED and the Senate estimate is -0.16.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The outcomes differ. The paper measures who earns lobbying fees, not where PAC money goes, and Furnas et al. separately show low overlap between organizations that lobby and organizations that give. A null SHIFT on PAC giving share is therefore not contradicted by a revenue premium for lobbying firms. If SHIFT is ever extended to lobbying, the paper suggests keying it to realized House control, with chambers stratified.

gaps_exposed: No firm-level partisan identity for lobbying registrants. Neither Melange nor Mentat derives a registrant's partisanship from its lobbyists' FEC giving, which the paper shows is reliable (kappa 0.84 to 0.86). If added, it may only be a descriptive identity attribute (D-021), never an edge or a weight.
The Mentat lobbying refit (dy ~ dg + factor(year)) has no partisan or control-change term, and the outside-firm fee series has not been checked for steps after House flips (2011, 2019).

No House-versus-Senate stratification for lobbying. The forecast and the sector study split chambers for giving share but not for lobbying revenue, the outcome where the paper finds the House-Senate asymmetry.

The system does not track bipartisan intermediaries among lobbying firms. The paper finds bipartisan firms earn the most, consistent with Bacik's bipartisan-lobbyist finding, but no firm-level bipartisanship measure exists.
flags: Denominator and window: the DV is real revenue per lobbyist per quarter. The 2011 difference-in-differences figures (+$10k Republican-aligned, more than -$40k Democratic-aligned) are one-year changes estimated on that outcome for 1,603 contract firms, 2008-2016. Quote them with that window and denominator, and never as sector totals or as a per-firm figure.

The revenue premium measures what clients pay for perceived majority access. Under D-025 it must not be restated as an access probability, a closeness measure or an influence weight. Under D-021, LDA-derived firm partisanship is identity only.

Citation hygiene: the cpf_pressure comment at fec/moneyball_core.py:10-11 cites 'Furnas/Bakker source-alignment'. That is not this paper. This paper offers no persuasion ratio and cannot calibrate the 1.7/0.5 constants.
The paper argues for neither of the rejected SNA proposals (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization).

Paul's seats-weekly position says 'neither paper on disk'. That is stale for this paper, which has now been read in full. His highlight records only the -$40k loss, not the asymmetric +$10k gain, and does not state that the figure is per lobbyist.

The SEATS-W sign is negative: the Democratic giving share falls as expected Democratic seats rise. This paper does not explain that result, so it must not be cited as corroborating access-seeking in SEATS-W.
paul_alignment: The evidence partly agrees with Paul's takeaway. His highlights (stable firm partisanship, a large loss for firms tied to the party that loses the House, weaker Senate ties, very few lobbyists moving between opposite-party firms) match the paper. Two points need correcting. First, the $40k figure is a one-year change on a per-lobbyist outcome and applies to Democratic-aligned firms. The matching gain for Republican-aligned firms was only about $10k, so the effect is asymmetric. Second, the paper concerns lobbying-fee revenue, not PAC giving. Paul's plan uses it, together with Cox & Magar, to motivate the seats test, but SEATS-W found a House response with the opposite sign to a 'chase the expected winner' reading, and SHIFT found no stable partisan shift. The paper therefore supports splitting by chamber, House versus Senate, and does not support the direction of the seat-gain hypothesis. His note that the paper is not on disk is stale, and his annotation entry for this work is empty.

extraction.research_question: Can the knowledge, skills and abilities needed for lobbying be taught to pre- and early-career lobbyists at the graduate professional level, and which parts cannot be taught (Executive Summary p.2; "What Can Be Taught" pp.8-19)?
extraction.theory: Lobbying is treated as a profession with a growing body of knowledge. Lobbyists' value rests on information lawmakers lack (Hula 1999; Hall and Deardorff 2006, as cited p.11-12), on being trusted agents for principals (Ainsworth and Sened 1993; Kersh 2002, p.13-14), and on reciprocal relationships built on mutual need (Wright 1996; Susman 2008, p.17). The authors divide teachable lobbying into three areas: knowledge (process, policy, analytic), communication and messaging, and relationship building. Relationship building is only partly teachable because it is tied to personality (p.17). Experience and personality are acknowledged as important but not sufficient (p.3-8).
extraction.data: No dataset, sample, unit of analysis, time window or N. Evidence is drawn from: (a) published figures cited from others, namely Rehr 2012 (about 30,000 DC lobbyists in 2012; survey finding on LDA/HLOGA knowledge) and LaPira and Thomas 2014 (revolving door), p.5 and p.10-11; (b) interviews cited in the text and notes, namely Dan Hurley (25 Aug 2014, n.1), Brad Fitch of the Congressional Management Foundation (4 Sep 2014, n.5), Alan Rosenblatt (11 Sep 2014, n.7), and a CMF communication from Nicole Folk Cooper (11 Sep 2014, n.5, on file, not published); (c) the authors' own experience, including past work in politics; (d) a Mike House quote from Goldman 2012 (p.3). Era of cited data: 2012-2014.
extraction.method: Qualitative and argumentative. Literature synthesis from political science on interest groups and lobbying, interview-informed claims, and personal experience, used to propose a graduate curriculum (seminars, simulations, capstone, internship or practicum). No statistical estimation, coding, or formal test of the proposed curriculum.
extraction.scope: US lobbying profession, centred on Washington DC federal lobbying (p.4-5), with brief mention of state, local and supranational institutions (p.25). Covers contract lobbyists, nonprofit advocates, grassroots managers, regulatory specialists, coalition brokers and PR consultants (p.4-5). Target population is pre- and early-career students in graduate professional programs, with undergraduate political science as a feeder (p.5-6, p.23). Campaign finance discussion is explicitly national (p.20).
extraction.identification: None. The paper makes no causal claims and has no identification strategy.

key_findings.finding: Central claim: much of lobbying, though not all, can be taught at graduate level. Three areas are proposed: knowledge (process, policy, analytic), communication and messaging, and relationship building.
key_findings.location: Executive Summary p.2; What Can Be Taught pp.8-19

key_findings.finding: Experience and personality limit what training can do; the authors argue good instincts are as much a product of training as of experience or natural ability.
Lobbyist population and career entry: of roughly 30,000 people who more or less were DC lobbyists in 2012, only 12 per cent are younger than 35 (Rehr 2012).
Revolving door: about 52 per cent of these lobbyists came through government, and 48 per cent of those held two or more government positions (LaPira and Thomas 2014, as cited).
key_findings.numbers: 52% revolving door; 48% of those with 2+ government positions

key_findings.finding: About 37 per cent of DC lobbyists surveyed by Rehr knew next to nothing about what the LDA and HLOGA required of them. The authors use this to argue for compliance training.
key_findings.numbers: 37% knew next to nothing about LDA/HLOGA

key_findings.finding: Congressional offices are overloaded: each office receives about a foot and a half of paper a day, plus email and social media (Congressional Management Foundation, cited).
key_findings.numbers: About 1.5 feet of paper per office per day

key_findings.finding: Campaign finance: the evidence on its impact is at best mixed (Baumgartner and Leech 1998). Very few lobbyists engage in campaign finance and those who do are partisan (Koger and Victor 2009). The authors conclude campaign finance matters less in lobbying than popular belief holds.

Five teachable relationship-building elements: (1) relationships rest on mutual need, not personal friendship; (2) relationships are targeted at lawmakers with a relevant interest; (3) lobbyists must look at ease socialising, including at fundraisers; (4) internships and practicums are where first professional networks form; (5) ethics, including honesty, confidentiality limits, and the lobbyist's primary duty to the client.

Networks and value: a lobbyist's market value, especially for a for-hire firm, is their portfolio of relationships (citing Blanes i Vidal et al. 2012). The authors warn these relationships can come to matter more to lobbyists than to the people they represent (citing Holyoke 2011).
Coalitions: lobbyists are more attractive to coalition partners when they bring information others lack and want (Hula 1999). Informed lobbyists also attract other lobbyists' attention.

Messaging and targeting: personalised messages are far more effective than duplicates (Fitch 2010); constituent messages with a personal story persuade members most; members of interest groups contact lawmakers more than non-members (Holyoke 2013); identical e-petitions are called worthless (Fitch 2009; Shih 2011).

Curriculum: teach lobbying mainly at graduate level, with continuing education later. Undergraduate courses should cover fundamentals and fold lobbying into existing classes. Graduate programmes should combine lectures and seminars, communication and PR courses (including social media), simulations, a capstone simulation with surprise shocks, and required internships or practicums.
key_findings.numbers: None; 'three thoughts ... not a steadfast instructional rule' (p.23)

key_findings.finding: Simulation modules are proposed in three groups: process (recruiting clients, budgeting, procedure), policy (strategy, stakeholder mapping, policy histories, state and international venues), and analytical (data collection, white papers, testimony, reporting).

limitations: No formal limitations section. The authors say not everything a lobbyist needs can be taught in the classroom, and that experience and personality matter (p.3-4, p.7-8).
Hedged claims: the five relationship-building elements are introduced with 'arguably' (p.17), and messaging recommendations are framed as 'suggests' (p.17).
Curricular recommendations are explicitly 'an approach, but not a steadfast instructional rule' (p.23). Nothing has been tested or evaluated.
Simulations 'often cannot capture the unexpected and unpredictable swings of political warfare' (p.23).
Authors question whether political scientists are prepared to teach professional writing (p.14).

Anecdotal support: the claim that short writing assignments are common comes from colleagues ('Or so we have heard', n.4, p.26). Interview claims are not independently verifiable (CMF communication 'on file ... available on request', n.5).
The ethics code of the American Government Relations Professionals binds only members, and there is little enforcement (n.6, p.26-27).
Key statistics (30,000 lobbyists, 12% under 35, 52% revolving door, 37% knowledge gap) are cited from secondary or association sources and are not re-derived by the authors.
Mentions 'cold cynicism' and other normative judgements without empirical support.

summary_md:
Holyoke, Brown and LaPira write a conceptual essay with a curriculum proposal. It is not an empirical study. They argue that most of lobbying can be taught at graduate level, in three areas: knowledge (process, policy and analytics), communication and messaging, and relationship building. Relationship building is only partly teachable because it depends on personality. The paper has no data, sample, window or tests. Every number it gives comes from someone else: about 30,000 DC lobbyists in 2012, 12% of them under 35 (Rehr 2012); 52% came through the revolving door (LaPira and Thomas 2014); 37% knew next to nothing about LDA/HLOGA. Its substantive claims are hedged with words like "arguably" and "suggests". They are: relationships rest on mutual need and are aimed at lawmakers with a relevant constituency stake, not on friendship; group members contact lawmakers more than non-members do; identical mass messages are worthless; campaign finance matters less than people think, and few lobbyists give at all.

The paper is weak evidence for Paul's systems. It is useful as framing, not calibration. Its sharpest bearing is on the staffer overlap router. In the code (`fec/surfaces/staffer_overlap_routes.py:33-39`), tie strength is proximity × log2(1 + shared days / 30) of dated co-work. The paper says a working relationship comes from mutual need and targeting, not from time spent in the same office. So the router's strength is at best a proxy for the chance of contact. Treat it as a heuristic cost, never as relationship strength or access (D-025). The paper also loosely backs three things: the flip model treating money as the minor channel; Terrier's Sphere of Influence using civic engagement; and the footprint version of Demographic Potential, through constituency-stake targeting. None of these backs any weight or constant.

bearings.system_side: Routes run through dated co-work, with strength = proximity x log2(1 + days/30) and distance = ceil(1e6 x 128 / strength). The overlay costs are: current co-worker 1, reported activity 2, historical 3, filing 5, policy 8. Shared tenure stands in for how usable a tie is.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Conceptual only. The paper never measures whether shared tenure produces usable relationships. It implies that co-work measures the opportunity for contact, not the mutual need that keeps a relationship going. Its revolving-door share is a federal DC figure from about 2012-2014 and fits the router's staff-to-lobbyist population. It does not support any cost constant or the log-days form. Route cost must stay a heuristic, not an introduction probability (D-025). No influence wording on revolving-door edges.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-pathfinding#Ordered person-overlap routes and employment-routing overlay|Ordered person-overlap routes and employment-routing overlay]]

bearings.paper_claim: Members of interest groups contact lawmakers more than non-members do (Holyoke 2013, cited). Entrenched interests show an issue's importance by having prominent constituents call first. Members should target their own elected officials, and personal constituent stories persuade most (Fitch 2010, cited).
bearings.system_side: Sphere of Influence = 100 x (0.10 household + 0.45 giving + 0.45 volunteering). Giving is built from charitable-donor, donor-index and high-contribution vendor fields. There is no term for group membership or prior contact with officials. The weights are Paul's 'leaning' ruling.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the direction carries over: civically engaged people are likelier to contact their own representative. The claims are cited, not tested, and are about national federal contact. Vendor charitable-giving fields are not the political group membership the paper names. Nothing here supports the 45/45/10 weights.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/terrier-row-scoring#Sphere of Influence|Sphere of Influence]]

bearings.paper_claim: Evidence on campaign finance's impact is at best mixed (Baumgartner and Leech 1998). 'Very few' lobbyists take part in campaign finance, and those who do are partisan (Koger and Victor 2009). The authors conclude that campaign money matters less to lobbying than popular belief holds. No figure is given.
bearings.system_side: pflip uses WM = 0.35 for money and WP = 0.65 for peer proximity. The code comment says money is the minority partner and buys access, not votes. Money terms saturate relative to receipts.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper agrees with the ordering (money below relationships and information) but gives no estimate. It relies on secondary sources from 1998-2009. It speaks about lobbyists' personal giving, not PAC money given to members, so it cannot calibrate the 0.35/0.65 split or HALFF.

bearings.paper_claim: Relationship targeting means finding lawmakers who respond to information and who have an electoral interest in the group's constituency (p.18). Lobbyists should pick out lawmakers with a relevant interest (p.17).
bearings.system_side: The default footprint mode scores a district's existing CU footprint (employment LQ, establishments, branches, deposits) and qualifies a district at employment LQ >= 1.0. Paul's ruling: 'the footprint should be the potential'. The weights are labelled judgmental and unestimated.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This matches the targeting logic only in concept: aim at members whose constituents hold a stake. The paper does not test whether that stake predicts responsiveness, and Demographic Potential does not feed Demo%. No weight support.
